events.name: Committee to find a lot for the African Church (Richard Allen, Absalom Jones, William Gray, William Wilcher)
events.location: Philadelphia: lot at Lombard and Sixth streets, then a lot in Fifth street
events.description: Richard Allen's own account. After the Methodist elder threatened to disown them, Allen and the Rev. Absalom Jones went out with a subscription paper for an African church and collected three hundred and sixty dollars the first day. "We appointed a committee to look out for a lot—the Rev. Absalom Jones, William Gray, William Wilcher and myself. We pitched upon a lot at the corner of Lombard and Sixth streets." Allen agreed for that lot with Mr. Mark Wilcox. The committee then bought a lot in Fifth street instead and left the first lot on Allen's hands; he kept it, and it became the site of Bethel. Allen "put the first spade in the ground to dig a cellar" for the African church, "the first African church or meeting-house that was erected in the United States of America." The members voted to unite with the Church of England, with only Allen and Jones voting Methodist. This African Church is the later St. Thomas African Episcopal Church; Allen does not use that name. || Source: Richard Allen, The Life, Experience, and Gospel Labors of the Rt. Rev. Richard Allen (Philadelphia, 1880), pp. 17-18. The book gives no date for the committee. The year 1793 is printed on p. 19, where a committee from the African Church asks Allen to be its minister. Scans: manuscripts/Allen_LifeExperience_1880/RA_1880_p17.jpg manuscripts/Allen_LifeExperience_1880/RA_1880_p18.jpg manuscripts/Allen_LifeExperience_1880/RA_1880_p19.jpg || Full book: https://archive.org/details/lifeexperiencego1880alle/page/16/mode/2up
attendees: lot committee; first proposer of the African church; agreed for the Lombard and Sixth street lot

events.name: Breaking ground for the African Church: Richard Allen puts the first spade in the ground
events.description: The beginning of the African Church, the church that became St. Thomas African Episcopal Church. Richard Allen's own account: "The day was appointed to go and dig the cellar. I arose early in the morning and addressed the throne of grace, praying that the Lord would bless our endeavors. Having by this time two or three teams of my own—as I was the first proposer of the African church, I put the first spade in the ground to dig a cellar for the same. This was the first African church or meeting-house that was erected in the United States of America." The lot was the one the committee had bought in Fifth street. The members then held an election and chose to unite with the Church of England; only Allen and the Rev. Absalom Jones voted for the Methodists. || Source: Richard Allen, The Life, Experience, and Gospel Labors of the Rt. Rev. Richard Allen (Philadelphia, 1880), pp. 17-18. Allen gives no date for the day itself; 1793 is the year printed on p. 19 for the African Church. He does not describe the opening service of the finished building, and he does not use the name St. Thomas. Scans: manuscripts/Allen_LifeExperience_1880/RA_1880_p17.jpg manuscripts/Allen_LifeExperience_1880/RA_1880_p18.jpg manuscripts/Allen_LifeExperience_1880/RA_1880_p19.jpg || Full book: https://archive.org/details/lifeexperiencego1880alle/page/16/mode/2up
attendees: put the first spade in the ground; first proposer of the African church

events.name: Opening of Bethel Church by Bishop Asbury
events.description: Richard Allen's own account of the founding of Bethel. He would not hinder the African Church in its building, but he remained a Methodist. "I bought an old frame that had been formerly occupied as a blacksmith shop, from Mr. Sims, and hauled it on the lot in Sixth near Lombard street, that had formerly been taken for the Church of England. I employed carpenters to repair the old frame, and fit it for a place of worship. In July 1794, Bishop Asbury being in town I solicited him to open the church for us which he accepted. The Rev. John Dickins sung and prayed, and Bishop Asbury preached. The house was called Bethel, agreeable to the prayer that was made." || Source: Richard Allen, The Life, Experience, and Gospel Labors of the Rt. Rev. Richard Allen (Philadelphia, 1880), pp. 19-20. Bishop Francis Asbury and the Rev. John Dickins were white Methodist ministers and are not entered as people here. attendees: founder; bought and fitted up the building
